rules.quote: The output is two Verilog files that can be instantiated by a peripheral that follows the Comportability Guidelines.
rules.statement: The tool output is two Verilog files that can be instantiated by a peripheral following the Comportability Guidelines.

rules.quote: As an example the tool can be invoked from the top project directory to generate the uart registers with:
rules.statement: The tool can be invoked from the top project directory to generate the uart registers.

rules.quote: The name_reg2hw_t structure contains the signals that are driven from the register module to the rest of the hardware (this contains any required .q, .qe, and .re signals described below).
rules.statement: The name_reg2hw_t structure contains the signals driven from the register module to the rest of the hardware, including required .q, .qe and .re signals.

rules.quote: The name_hw2reg_t structure contains the signals that are driven from the rest of the hardware to the register module (this contains any required .d and .de signals described below).
rules.statement: The name_hw2reg_t structure contains the signals driven from the rest of the hardware to the register module, including required .d and .de signals.

rules.quote: Accesses to unmapped target addresses that can be fully represented with the internally used address bits typically return an error.
rules.condition: access to an unmapped address representable with the internally used address bits
rules.statement: Accesses to unmapped target addresses fully representable with internal address bits typically return an error.

rules.quote: If the resulting address is mapped, the request is forwarded to the corresponding register and no error is returned. No error is returned for this request.
rules.condition: excess address bits map the request to a mapped address, e.g. 0x184 to 0x84
rules.statement: If the stripped address is mapped, the request is forwarded to the register and no error is returned.

rules.quote: A request to address 0x88 can be represented using the 8 internal address bits but there is no register mapped at this address. Typical implementations return an error for such a request.
rules.condition: module registers span 0x0 to 0x84 with 8 internal address bits; request to unmapped address 0x88
rules.statement: A request to unmapped address 0x88 typically returns an error.

rules.quote: TL-UL a_opcode illegal value
rules.statement: An error response is returned when TL-UL a_opcode has an illegal value.

rules.quote: TL-UL writes of size smaller than register size This can be seen with an 8b write to a register which is larger than 8 bits, or a 16b write to a register which is larger than 16 bits.
rules.condition: TL-UL write of size smaller than the register size, e.g. 8b write to a register wider than 8 bits
rules.statement: A write smaller than the register size must return an error.

rules.quote: TL-UL writes of size smaller than 32b that are not word-aligned I.e. writes of size 8b or 16b that are not to an address that is 4B aligned return in error.
rules.condition: 8b or 16b write to an address not 4B aligned
rules.statement: Writes smaller than 32b that are not word-aligned must return an error.

rules.quote: Reads of size smaller than full word (32b) return the full register content and do not signal error.
rules.statement: Reads smaller than a full word return the full register content and do not signal an error.

rules.quote: Reads response data is always in its byte-channel, i.e. a one-byte read to address 0x3 will return the full word with the correct MSB in bits [31:24] on the TL-UL response bus (as well as the not-asked-for bytes 2:0 in [23:0]).
rules.statement: Read response data is always in its byte channel, e.g. a one-byte read to 0x3 returns the full word with the correct byte in bits [31:24].

rules.quote: It is recommended to follow the above error rules based on the declared number of validbits: for the window, but there are some cases where this might be relaxed.
rules.statement: Windows should follow the error rules based on the declared validbits, though this may be relaxed in some cases.

rules.quote: This is typically the same as q[] except for hwext registers. de input Hardware data enable from peripheral logic, scalar, should be set when the hardware wishes to update the register field d[] input Hardware data from peripheral logic, size == field size qe output Output register enable, scalar, true when bus interface writes to subreg q[] output Output register content, size == field size.
rules.statement: The qs output is typically the same as q except for hwext registers.

rules.quote: Coming in from the left (bus) are the software write enable and write data, which has the highest priority in modifying the register contents. If both software and hardware request an update in the same clock cycle (i.e. both de and we are true), the software updated value is used, as shown in the diagram.
rules.condition: software and hardware request an update in the same clock cycle (de and we both true)
rules.statement: The software-written value takes priority over the hardware update.

rules.quote: Optionally, if the hwaccess attribute allows writes from the hardware, the hardware can present updated values in the form of data enable (de) and update data (d).
rules.statement: The hardware can present updated values through de and d.

rules.quote: If the data enable is true, the register content is updated with the update data.
rules.condition: de is true and no software write
rules.statement: The register content is updated with d.

rules.quote: Finally an attribute value of none asks for no interface to the hardware, and might be used for things like scratch registers or DV test registers where only software can modify the value, or informational registers like version numbers that are read-only by the software.
rules.statement: A hwaccess of none requests no hardware interface, usable for scratch, DV test or read-only version registers.

rules.quote: Another attribute in the register description hwqe, when true indicates that the hardware wants to see the software write enable exported to the peripheral logic. This is just a registered version of the bus side write-enable we so that its rising edge aligns with the change in the q output.
rules.statement: qe is a registered version of the bus write enable we, aligned with the change in q.

rules.quote: Finally, note that no de input is required from the rest of the peripheral hardware, only the d is added to the struct bundle.
rules.statement: No de input is required from hardware; only d is added to the struct bundle.

rules.section_title: Type RO, with hwext and zero-gate options
rules.quote: Read-only type registers can be thought of as identical as RW types with no wd and we input.
rules.statement: RO registers behave as RW registers with no wd and we inputs.

rules.section_title: Type RO, with hwext and zero-gate options
rules.quote: In this case, a hardwired value is returned for a software read equal to the default value assigned to the register this can be useful for auto-generated register values with no storage register required.
rules.condition: swaccess is ro, hwaccess is none or hro, and hwext is true
rules.statement: A software read returns a hardwired value equal to the register default value.

rules.quote: This signal re indicates that this register is being read, in which case the contents should be set to zero.
rules.statement: When re indicates the register is being read, the register contents are set to zero.

rules.quote: Note this register is not recommended but might be required for backwards compatibility to other IP functionality.
rules.statement: RC registers are not recommended, except for backwards compatibility with other IP.

rules.quote: At the moment hwext is not allowed to be true for RC since there is no exporting of the re signal. If this is required, please add a feature request.
rules.statement: hwext must not be true for RC registers since re is not exported.

rules.quote: If there is no storage required, only an indication of the act of writing, then hwext should be set to true and the outside hardware can handle the write event.
rules.condition: WO register needing no storage, only write indication
rules.statement: hwext should be set to true so outside hardware handles the write event.

rules.section_title: Type R0W1C, RW1S, RW1C and RW0C
rules.quote: Certain RW register types must be implemented with special configuration of prim_subreg since the act of writing causes the values to be set in unique ways.
rules.statement: These register types must be implemented with special prim_subreg configuration because writing sets values in unique ways.

rules.quote: As shown in the module descriptions, the subreg needs to handle the case when both hardware and software attempt to write at the same time.
rules.condition: hardware and software attempt to write the register at the same time
rules.statement: The subreg for R0W1C/RW1S/RW1C/RW0C types must handle simultaneous hardware and software write attempts.

rules.quote: As is true with the RW type, the software has precedence, but it is more tricky here.
rules.statement: Software has precedence over hardware, as for the RW type.

rules.quote: In this description if the hardware is writing, its value is sent to the logic that potentially clears that value or the stored value.
rules.condition: hardware is writing a RW1C register
rules.statement: The hardware value is sent to the logic that potentially clears that value or the stored value.

rules.quote: The recommendation is that the hardware feed the q value back into d, only setting bits with new events. Then there will be no "collision" between hardware setting events and software clearing events.
rules.statement: Hardware should feed the q value back into d, only setting bits with new events, to avoid collisions with software clearing.

rules.quote: But if the event is still true (the HW d input is still 1) then the clear should still have effect for one cycle in order to create a new interrupt edge. Since d is still 1 the q will return to 1 after one cycle, since the clean up was not successful.
rules.condition: software clears a RW1C bit while the hardware d input is still 1
rules.statement: The software clear must still take effect for one cycle to create a new interrupt edge, then q returns to 1 since d is still 1.

rules.quote: It is legal to create RW1C, RW1S, etc. with hwext true.
rules.statement: RW1C, RW1S and similar register types may be created with hwext true.

rules.quote: In these cases the auto-generated hardware is simply the same as the hwext RW register shown earlier. This causes all of the implementation to be done outside of the generated register block.
rules.condition: RW1C, RW1S or similar register has hwext true
rules.statement: The auto-generated hardware is the same as the hwext RW register, with the implementation done outside the generated register block.

rules.quote: Similarly it is legal to set hwqe true for any of these register types if the clearing wants to be monitored by the hardware outside.
rules.condition: clearing is to be monitored by external hardware
rules.statement: hwqe may be set true for these register types.

skipped.text: The goal for these types of registers is to have software clear or set certain bits at the same time hardware is clearing or setting other bits.
So in theory what software is clearing, hardware is setting, or vice-versa.
An example would be where hardware is setting interrupt status bits, and software is clearing them, using RW1C.
The logic for RW1C shows how this is implemented in the module:
So if the hardware accidentally clears fields that the software hasn't cleared yet, there is a risk that events will not be seen by software.

The HW could have chosen to simply treat d and de as set-only, but the preference is to leave the subreg simple and allow the hardware to do either "the right thing" or whatever it feels is appropriate for its needs.
(Perhaps it is a feature to clear all events in the hardware.)
The one "conflict" that is common and worth mentioning is RW1C on an interrupt vector.
This is the typical scenario where hardware sets bits (representing an interrupt event), and software clears bits (indicating the event has been handled).
The assumption is that between the hardware setting and software clearing, software has cleaned up whatever caused the event in the first place.
There is no way to guarantee that hardware is doing the right thing, but at least the RW1C conveys the notion to software the intended effect.
